name: Picosecond laser (PicoSure/PicoWay)

card.summary: Ultra-short-pulse laser used for pigment, tattoos and acne scars; small prospective studies report scar improvement, with few large trials.
card.note: Clinic-performed; the main scar study was small, uncontrolled and limited to skin types III-IV.

quick.overview:
Picosecond lasers deliver energy in trillionths of a second. PicoSure and PicoWay are commercial devices of this type, used in clinics for tattoo and pigment treatment, skin texture and acne scars.

Published evidence for acne scars is limited to small prospective studies; a 2020 study of 18 completers reported improvement in scar grading scores after six sessions. Registered trials also cover wrinkles, melasma and skin tightening.
quick.mechanism: A fractionated picosecond laser creates tiny zones of injury in the epidermis. A microscopy study in one volunteer found micro-injuries concentrated in pigmented cells, with debris exfoliated over about four weeks, suggesting melanin as the main absorber of the beam.
quick.risks: The 2020 acne scar study concluded the treatment was safe in 18 patients with skin types III-IV, but no large safety dataset was identified, and pain was measured as an outcome. Results in other skin types are not covered. Treatments are performed in clinics.

lead: Picosecond lasers are lasers whose pulses last a trillionth of a second, shorter than earlier nanosecond devices. PicoSure and PicoWay are among the commercial systems clinics use for pigmented lesions, tattoos, skin texture and acne scars. Registered trials cover tattoos, melasma, wrinkles, skin quality and facial laxity [3][4][5][6][7][8].

For acne scars, a 2020 prospective study of a fractionated dual-wavelength picosecond laser reported improvement in physician-rated scar scores and patient-rated scores; the authors said few prospective studies of this device in acne scars had been published [1]. A 2017 imaging study described how fractionated non-ablative picosecond treatment injures skin on a microscopic level [2].
Evidence is small-scale: the studies identified here are one prospective study with 18 completers and one single-volunteer descriptive study.
infobox: Acne scars, pigment, tattoos, wrinkles, laxity

paras: In a 2017 study, a fractionated non-ablative picosecond laser was applied to the arm of one volunteer and imaged with multiphoton microscopy over four weeks. The study reported micro-injuries in the epidermis, damaged pigmented cells that suggested melanin as the main absorber for laser-induced optical breakdown, inflammatory cells near the injuries after 24 hours, and exfoliation of the injuries over four weeks. It was described as observational groundwork rather than evidence of clinical benefit [2].

A prospective study enrolled 20 patients with skin types III-IV with acne scars; 18 completed six monthly sessions with both 532 nm and 1,064 nm fractionated handpieces. Physician-assessed scar grading scores fell from 15.22 to 10.61 for quantity and from 3.00 to 2.33 for quality, and patient visual analogue scores fell from 4.28 to 2.00, all reported as statistically significant. The authors concluded the approach was efficacious and safe, without a control group [1].

Registered trials include studies of picosecond lasers for tattoo removal with 60 participants (completed) [3], melasma with 40 participants (completed) [4], wrinkles using a specialised lens array in two 20-participant studies (completed) [5][6], skin quality [7], and facial skin tightening with a fractional 1,064 nm device [8]. The registry entries loaded for this article do not list results.
The laser is categorised on the wiki under hardmaxx for scars and marks. No community threads are cited in this article.
